body.working_title: Good practice for evaluating predictions: what the literature supports

body.text: Brief requirements (from the supervisor, 2026-11-13): (1) a claimset based on prediction.md of entrylib/study-planning (v0.2, commit 104ba1c); (2) a pure literature summary: each claim is a statement of good practice supported by the paper(s) it rests on, no new computation; (3) one claim per default and one per Avoid item (supervisor's choice); (4) what not to do is stated as separate claims, with references; (5) papers cited by DOI, captured from open-access copies where they can be reached (supervisor's choice); (6) kept in the lab, on branch claimset/prediction-good-practice of entrylib/study-planning.

Which measures and tests should a study use to evaluate and compare predictions (point forecasts of a mean, a median or a quantile, prediction intervals, predictive distributions, class probabilities), according to the methodological literature on evaluating forecasts and classifiers?

body.definition: A scoring function (an error measure for point forecasts) is consistent for a functional of the predictive distribution, such as the mean, the median or a quantile, when its expected value is lowest when the point forecast equals that functional.

A scoring rule for probabilistic forecasts is proper when its expected value is best when the forecast distribution equals the distribution of the outcome, and strictly proper when it is best only then.
A single-valued forecast meant to equal the mean (expected value) of the outcome's distribution given the information available.
A single-valued forecast meant to equal the median of the outcome's distribution given the information available.
Root mean squared error: the square root of the mean of the squared differences between outcomes and point forecasts.
Root mean squared scaled error: the RMSE of a series' forecasts divided by the in-sample RMSE of the one-step naive forecast of that series, so that series on different scales can be averaged.
Mean absolute error: the mean of the absolute differences between outcomes and point forecasts.
Mean absolute scaled error: the MAE of a series' forecasts divided by the in-sample MAE of the one-step naive forecast of that series.
Mean absolute percentage error: the mean of the absolute differences between outcomes and point forecasts, each divided by the outcome.
Symmetric mean absolute percentage error: the mean of the absolute differences between outcomes and point forecasts, each divided by the mean of the absolute outcome and the absolute forecast.
The beta-median with beta = -1: the point forecast that minimises the expected absolute percentage error; for positive outcomes it lies below the median.
The quantile (asymmetric piecewise linear) loss at level tau: tau times the error when the outcome is above the forecast, and (1 - tau) times the absolute error when it is below.
The score of a central (1 - alpha) prediction interval: its width plus 2/alpha times the distance by which the outcome falls outside it.
The share of outcomes that fall inside the prediction intervals, compared with their nominal level.
Continuous ranked probability score: the integral over thresholds of the squared difference between the forecast's cumulative distribution function and the step function at the outcome.
The logarithmic score: the negative logarithm of the forecast density (or probability) at the outcome.
The mean squared difference between forecast probabilities of a class and the outcome coded 1 if the class occurred and 0 otherwise.
The value of the forecast's cumulative distribution function at the outcome; for a calibrated forecast its values are uniformly distributed.
Statistical consistency between forecast distributions and outcomes: events forecast with a given probability occur with that frequency.
The concentration of the forecast distributions, a property of the forecasts alone; among calibrated forecasts, sharper ones are better.
The share of cases whose predicted class, after thresholding the predicted probabilities, equals the observed class.
The area under the ROC curve: the probability that a randomly chosen case of the positive class receives a higher score than a randomly chosen case of the negative class.
The curve of precision (the share of predicted positives that are positive) against recall (the share of positives predicted as positive) over the classification thresholds.
A time series with many zero values, such as the sales of a slow-moving item.
A non-parametric test of whether several methods differ, applied to their ranks on each of several data sets.
A post-hoc test after the Friedman test that compares every pair of methods by their mean ranks against a critical difference.
Multiple comparisons with the best: a test, on mean ranks over series, of which methods differ significantly from the best-ranked one.
A test of equal expected loss of two competing forecasts of the same series, based on the mean loss differential and its long-run variance.
Correcting a forecast back-transformed from a Box-Cox or log scale so that it estimates the mean, not the median, of the forecast distribution.
Exponential smoothing state space models with error, trend and seasonal components, each additive, multiplicative or absent.

body.statement: To evaluate point forecasts, use a [[TM1:consistent scoring function]] for the functional the forecasts target (the mean, the median or a quantile): a scoring function consistent for a different functional rewards a different forecast from the one the method was built to make.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM1
conditions: the functional the forecasts target is known

body.statement: Point forecasts of the mean ([[TM3:point forecast of the mean]]) should be evaluated with squared error ([[TM5:RMSE]]), the scoring function consistent for the mean.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: When [[TM3:point forecasts of the mean]] are compared over series on different scales, the [[TM5:RMSE]] of each series should be scaled by the in-sample RMSE of the one-step naive forecast ([[TM6:RMSSE]]), as the M5 accuracy competition did; scaling each series by a fixed number keeps the comparison consistent for the mean.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: The point forecasts of [[TM30:ETS]] models are [[TM3:point forecasts of the mean]] (conditional means of the forecast distribution), except, beyond one step ahead, for models with a multiplicative trend or multiplicative seasonality.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM30
conditions: additive trend and seasonality, or one step ahead

body.statement: Point forecasts made on a Box-Cox or log scale and transformed back to the original scale are [[TM4:point forecasts of the median]], not of the mean, unless they are bias-adjusted ([[TM29:bias adjustment]]).
body.question: Q1

body.statement: [[TM7:MAE]] and [[TM8:MASE]] should not be the main measure for [[TM3:point forecasts of the mean]]: absolute error is consistent for the median and rewards median forecasts.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM7
about.relation: should not be the main measure for

body.statement: [[TM9:MAPE]] should not be the measure for point forecasts of the mean or the median: it is consistent for the [[TM11:median of order -1]], which lies below the median for positive outcomes, so it rewards forecasts that are too low.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM9
about.relation: should not be the measure for
about.object: point forecasts of the mean or the median

body.statement: [[TM10:sMAPE]] should not be the measure for point forecasts: it penalises errors of the same size differently depending on their sign, and it is undefined when the outcome and the forecast are both zero.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM10
about.relation: should not be the measure for

body.statement: Point forecasts of the median ([[TM4:point forecast of the median]]) should be evaluated with absolute error ([[TM7:MAE]]), the scoring function consistent for the median, and, across series on different scales, with [[TM8:MASE]].
body.question: Q1

body.statement: On [[TM24:intermittent series]], absolute-error measures should not be used alone: the median of the outcome can be zero, and absolute error then rewards a forecast of zero for every period.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: absolute-error measures
about.relation: should not be used alone on

body.statement: Quantile forecasts should be evaluated with the [[TM12:pinball loss]] at the quantile's level, the scoring function consistent for that quantile, averaged over the levels when there are several, and scaled per series when series are on different scales.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: Prediction intervals should be evaluated with the [[TM13:interval score]], a proper scoring rule for central intervals, reported together with their [[TM14:coverage]] against the nominal level.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: [[TM14:coverage]] alone should not be the measure of prediction intervals: it does not measure their width, so sharp intervals and needlessly wide ones can reach the same coverage.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM14
about.relation: should not be the only measure of

body.statement: Predictive distributions should be evaluated with a [[TM2:proper scoring rule]], such as the [[TM15:CRPS]] or the [[TM16:log score]].
body.question: Q1

body.statement: The evaluation of predictive distributions should check their [[TM19:calibration]], with the [[TM18:probability integral transform]] or coverage at several levels, and report their [[TM20:sharpness]]: the goal is the sharpest forecast that is calibrated.
body.question: Q1

body.statement: Predictive distributions of counts, such as forecasts of intermittent sales, should be evaluated with proper scoring rules and a randomised [[TM18:probability integral transform]], since the probability integral transform of a discrete forecast is not uniform even when the forecast is calibrated.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: proper scoring rules and the randomised PIT

body.statement: Forecast probabilities of classes should be evaluated with a [[TM2:proper scoring rule]], such as the [[TM16:log score]] or the [[TM17:Brier score]].
body.question: Q1

body.statement: [[TM21:accuracy]] should not be the measure of forecast class probabilities: it ignores the probabilities beyond which side of a threshold they fall, and weighs every error the same.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM21

conditions: predictions are probabilities, or the costs of errors differ

body.statement: [[TM22:AUC]] should not be the measure of forecast class probabilities: it measures how well cases are ranked, not whether the probabilities are right, and it weighs the costs of misclassification differently for different classifiers.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM22
about.relation: should not be the measure of

body.statement: With rare positive cases, the [[TM23:precision-recall curve]] should be reported rather than the ROC curve alone, because the ROC curve can look good while most cases predicted positive are negative.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: TM23
about.relation: is more informative than the ROC curve for

body.statement: When the compared methods target different functionals (one the mean, another the median), each should be evaluated with a measure consistent for its own target, or the methods made to target the same functional, because a single measure favours the methods that target what it is consistent for.
body.question: Q1

about.subject: the comparison of methods with different targets
